title: Book 7 — Polymnia, Chapter 129
paragraphs: Thessaly, it is said, was in old times a lake, enclosed on all sides by very lofty mountains; for the parts of it lying to the east are shut in by the ranges of Pelion and Ossa, which join each other at their lower slopes, those to the north by Olympus, those to the west by Pindus, and those to the south by Othrys. The region in the middle, between all these named mountains, is Thessaly, forming as it were a hollow. Many rivers flow into it — especially five of note: the Peneios, Apidanus, Onochonos, Enipeus, and Pamisos — which gather their waters from the mountains that ring Thessaly and run into the plain with separate names, finally flowing into the sea by one single narrow channel, after mingling all their waters together. As soon as they are mingled, the Peneios prevails over the rest with its name and obliterates the separate names. It is said that in ancient times, when this channel and outlet between the mountains did not yet exist, these rivers, together with Lake Boebeis, had no names as they do now; but by their waters they made the whole of Thessaly into a sea. The Thessalians themselves say that Poseidon made the channel through which the Peneios flows; and reasonably so, since anyone who believes that it is Poseidon who shakes the earth and that the chasms produced by earthquakes are his work would, on seeing this place, say that it was made by Poseidon — for the parting of the mountains is clearly, to my mind, the work of an earthquake.
